postTitle: Generation Gap: How Gen Z, Millennials and Boomers Choose Small Dining Sets
postContent:
In a small dining space the base matters more than the tabletop. A round pedestal table of 90cm will seat four people in a corner where a 120cm four leg table seats two in comfort and blocks the route to the kitchen, because the pedestal removes the legs that dictate where chairs can go. Anyone shopping for a compact set should decide the base type before anything else.

The second finding concerns what happens when the meal is over. Small dining sets are used for perhaps ninety minutes a day and occupy the room for the other twenty two and a half hours, so the seating has to disappear. Chairs that tuck fully under, benches that slide away and drop leaf tops that fold against a wall are what separate a set that works in a flat from one that has to be squeezed past.

Key findings at a glance

  • Pedestal and trestle bases seat more people in a given footprint than four leg tables, because chairs can be positioned anywhere around the edge.
  • Allow 75cm behind a chair to push back and stand in a compact room, and 100cm on any side that doubles as a walkway.
  • A round table of 90cm to 100cm seats four. A square table of 80cm seats four at a squeeze and two comfortably.
  • Placing one side of the table against a wall removes an entire clearance zone and is often the difference between a set fitting and not fitting.
  • Benches push fully under the table and store no air, which makes them the most space efficient seating in a narrow kitchen diner.
  • Drop leaf and folding tables give a room two identities, provided the closed position is genuinely usable rather than a compromise.
  • The Nationally Described Space Standard sets minimum internal floor areas for new homes where a local authority applies it, and those areas have to cover living, kitchen and dining space together.

How small a dining space can honestly be

There is no national dataset describing the size of UK dining spaces, and we are not going to invent one. What can be set out precisely is the floor area each configuration requires, which is the figure that actually determines whether a set fits. The table below uses 75cm of clearance per used side, the compact working figure, and notes what changes when a table is placed against a wall.

Set typeTable sizeSeatsFloor area to allowWhere it works
Round pedestal, two seater60cm to 70cm diameter22.1m x 2.1m free standing, 1.4m x 2.1m against a wallStudio flats and kitchen corners
Square, two to four seater80cm x 80cm2 to 42.3m x 2.3m free standingSquare kitchen diners
Round pedestal, four seater90cm to 100cm diameter42.5m x 2.5m free standingRooms with traffic passing on more than one side
Rectangular, four seater120cm x 75cm42.7m x 2.3m free standing, 2.7m x 1.5m against a wallLong narrow terraced rooms
Drop leaf, two to four seater80cm closed, 120cm open2 closed, 4 openVaries with the setting in useFlats where the room changes role during the day
Rectangular with bench120cm x 75cm4, with two on the bench2.7m x 1.6m with the bench on the wall sideKitchen diners with a single usable wall

Those figures assume a compact room. Where space allows, extend the clearance to 100cm on the sides people walk past, since the difference between 75cm and 100cm is the difference between edging round a seated diner and passing them without contact.

Why the base decides everything

A four leg table places a fixed obstacle at each corner. Seat four people and every chair is negotiating a leg, which is why compact four leg tables so often seat two in practice. A pedestal base clears the perimeter entirely and lets chairs sit wherever they are needed, including on the diagonal, which is how a 90cm round table takes four without crowding.

Trestle and A frame bases sit between the two, keeping the corners free but restricting the middle of each long side. In a room where the table has to be pushed against a wall, a base with two supports at the ends is usually easier to live with than four legs, because it allows a chair to sit centrally on the exposed side.

Round tops bring a second advantage in tight rooms: there are no corners at hip height. In a galley kitchen or a narrow diner where people pass the table constantly while carrying things, that detail reduces daily friction more than any amount of clever storage. Two seater arrangements drawn from a range of bistro sets UK flats and kitchen corners can take are built around exactly this principle.

Three households, three compact briefs

Younger households are typically fitting dining into a room that was never designed for it: a corner of a studio, the end of a galley kitchen, a section of a shared living room. The table doubles as a desk, so the closed setting has to be usable all day, not merely tolerable. Light reflective surfaces help a small room read as larger, and a compact set with a gloss or glass top from a range of 4 seater glass dining table sets UK flats are furnished with keeps the floor visible and the space open.

Family households in smaller terraced homes have a different constraint: four people need to sit at once, every day, in a room that also contains the kitchen. Here a bench on the wall side is the most efficient answer, because two children can share it, it pushes fully under and nobody has to walk behind it. Options among dining benches UK kitchen diners are planned around free up the walkway that four separate chairs would consume. Durability of the top is the other priority, since a small table absorbs the same wear as a large one in a fraction of the surface area.

Households that have downsized are solving the problem in reverse. They are used to a full sized dining table and are choosing something smaller without giving up the ability to host. The priority becomes chair comfort rather than chair count, because a set of four supportive chairs used for long sittings beats six that are only ever half occupied. Solid construction remains the benchmark for this group, and sets drawn from 4 seater wooden dining table sets UK homes are downsized into tend to outlast the room they were bought for.

What happens between meals

The seating decision in a small room is really a storage decision. Chairs that tuck fully under the apron return their floor area to the room. Chairs with arms rarely do. Stacking chairs can be moved out entirely when the table becomes a desk, and folding chairs go flat against a wall or into a cupboard.

Drop leaf and folding tables extend the same logic to the top. They work well provided the closed setting still holds a laptop or a place setting, because a closed table that is unusable simply becomes a shelf. Test the mechanism by opening and closing it a few times: any table that takes real effort will stay in one position permanently, which defeats the purpose.

Wall colour and finish do more work in these rooms than people expect. A pale, reflective top bounces light back into a small space, which is why compact high gloss designs, such as those in high gloss dining table and 4 chairs UK ranges, suit basement kitchens and north facing rooms where light is short.

What this means for UK homes

Measure the gap, not the room. Establish the largest rectangle of floor the dining set can occupy, then subtract 75cm from each side that people will use, and choose from what remains. Decide immediately whether one side can go against a wall, since that single move often unlocks a set two sizes larger.

Choose a pedestal or end supported base wherever four people need to sit. Favour round tops in rooms with passing traffic and rectangular tops in long narrow rooms. Make sure every chair tucks fully under, and consider a bench on the wall side where children are involved. Then check the closed position of any folding design and be honest about whether you will use it daily. A small set chosen this way will feel generous, while a slightly larger one chosen without the clearances will feel like an obstacle from the first week.

Methodology

This 2026 report is based on the editorial assessment of Furniture in Fashion as a UK modern furniture retailer, standard furniture dimensions and the clearance figures used in room planning, together with published UK housing context named where it applies. No proprietary sales data, search data or customer records were used, and no survey fieldwork was carried out. Where national data on dining space dimensions does not exist, the report states that plainly and works from specification instead.

Citing this report

Media and websites may cite this analysis with credit to Furniture in Fashion as the publisher and a link to Furniture in Fashion. Please describe it as editorial research based on retail experience and standard specifications rather than as survey research.

Frequently asked questions

What is the smallest table that seats four?

A round pedestal table of 90cm to 100cm in diameter, or a square table of 80cm at a squeeze. The pedestal base is what makes four places workable, because no chair is competing with a leg.

How much clearance does a small dining set need?

Seventy five centimetres behind each chair that is used, extending to 100cm on any side that doubles as a walkway. Placing one side against a wall removes a clearance zone entirely and frees up considerable floor.

Are round or rectangular tables better in a small kitchen?

Round tables suit rooms where people walk past the table, since there are no corners at hip height. Rectangular tables suit long narrow rooms and can be pushed against a wall between meals.

Do benches save space at a dining table?

Yes. A bench pushes fully under the table, needs no walkway behind it when placed on a wall side, and seats children flexibly. It is the most space efficient seating available for a compact kitchen diner.

Are drop leaf tables worth it in a flat?

They are, provided the closed setting is genuinely usable for everyday meals or work. Test the mechanism before buying, because a table that is awkward to open will stay in one position and lose its advantage.

postTitle: Generation Gap: How Gen Z, Millennials and Boomers Choose Sofas
postContent:
Seat depth is the measurement that decides whether a sofa is comfortable, and it is the one almost nobody checks before buying. A depth of 60cm or more invites lying down and forces most people to add cushions if they want to sit upright. A depth of 50cm to 55cm supports the back without help. Neither is better in the abstract, but choosing the wrong one for the household is why so many sofas end up buried under scatter cushions doing a job the frame should have done.

Across the age groups, the differences we see are differences in posture and permanence. Younger buyers are furnishing rooms they will leave, so they weigh portability and configurability heavily. Households in the middle of family life buy for capacity and for covers that survive daily use. Older buyers are the most exacting about seat height and support, because the sofa has to be easy to leave as well as pleasant to sit in.

Key findings at a glance

  • Seat depth of 50cm to 55cm suits upright sitting. Depths of 60cm and above suit lounging and need cushions to support an upright posture.
  • Seat height of 45cm to 50cm makes standing up straightforward for most adults, and lower seats make it noticeably harder.
  • Leave about 90cm of walkway on the main route past a sofa, and 40cm to 45cm between the sofa and a coffee table.
  • A sofa should leave 15cm to 20cm of breathing space at each end of the wall it sits against, otherwise the room reads as full.
  • Frame construction, spring system and cushion fill determine how a sofa ages, and none of the three is visible in a photograph.
  • All upholstered furniture sold for domestic use in the UK must meet the Furniture and Furnishings (Fire) (Safety) Regulations 1988, and the permanent label should be present on the piece.
  • No published UK dataset breaks sofa buying down by generation, so the patterns described here are read from housing circumstances and stated priorities rather than presented as measured findings.

Depth, height and the way people actually sit

Sofa comfort is a fit problem. If the seat is deeper than the distance from the back of the sitter's hips to the back of their knees, they either slide forward and lose back support or fill the gap with cushions. If it is shallower, the front edge presses under the thigh. Height works the same way: a seat that is too low means the knees sit above the hips, which is relaxing for twenty minutes and tiring for two hours.

Back height decides whether the sofa supports the shoulders or the head. A low back reads as contemporary and keeps sightlines open in a small room, but it offers nothing above the shoulder blades. A high back supports the neck, which matters for anyone who dozes in front of the television. The table below maps the main dimensions to the way people sit.

How the sofa is usedSeat depthSeat heightBack heightCushion fill that suits
Upright sitting, conversation, short evenings50cm to 55cm45cm to 48cm85cm to 95cmFirm foam
Relaxed evening viewing55cm to 60cm43cm to 46cm80cm to 90cmFoam with a fibre wrap
Lounging and lying down60cm to 70cm40cm to 43cm70cm to 80cm plus scatter cushionsFeather or fibre, plumped regularly
Support for standing up easily50cm to 55cm46cm to 50cm90cm or more with head supportHigh resilience foam
Everyday family use55cm to 60cm44cm to 47cm85cm to 95cmHigh resilience foam with removable covers

Take the measurements yourself rather than trusting a description. Sit right back with your spine against the back cushion: if your feet do not sit flat on the floor and your knees do not bend over the front edge, the sofa is the wrong depth for you, whatever it looks like.

What is under the upholstery

Three things determine how a sofa ages, and none is visible in a picture. The frame is the first. Kiln dried hardwood resists the warping and movement that untreated timber suffers in a centrally heated home, and corner blocks and screwed joints hold up better than staples alone. Ask what the frame is made from before asking anything about the fabric.

The suspension is the second. Serpentine springs give a firmer, more supportive feel and hold their shape well. Elasticated webbing is lighter and softer and is common in slimmer contemporary designs. Both work, but they age differently, and webbing on a heavily used family sofa will show sag before a sprung platform does.

The fill is the third and the most noticeable day to day. High resilience foam keeps its shape with minimal effort. Feather is soft and enveloping but has to be plumped, sometimes daily, or the sofa looks tired within a week of a deep clean. Fibre sits between the two and flattens more quickly than either. Households that will not plump cushions should buy foam and accept a firmer seat, since the alternative is a sofa that always looks unmade. Across a range of modern sofas UK living rooms are furnished with, these three specifications explain most of the difference in how two similar looking pieces feel after three years.

Three households, three priorities

In first and rented homes the sofa has to be movable, and it is often the largest thing in the room. Two seaters and compact three seaters do most of the work, since they can be turned, carried up a staircase and rehomed in a differently shaped room later. Modular designs that split into single units are the strongest answer where access is uncertain. Seating that can be arranged and rearranged, including pieces such as tub chairs UK flats use to add a seat without adding a second sofa, gives a small room flexibility that a fixed suite cannot.

Family households buy for capacity and for cleaning. A three seater with generous seat depth absorbs children, adults and everything else that lands on it, and removable machine washable covers turn a spill from a crisis into a chore. Tight weaves resist snagging from pets and toys, and darker or textured cloths disguise daily marks better than flat pale ones. Sizing options among 3 seater fabric sofas UK family rooms are built around cover most of this group's requirements, provided the seat depth is chosen for adults rather than for photographs.

In long settled homes the sofa is judged on posture and durability. A higher, firmer seat, a supportive back and arms of a height that can be pushed against when standing are practical requirements rather than preferences. Leather suits this pattern because it wipes clean, ages gracefully and does not need laundering, and a pair of 2 seater leather sofas UK sitting rooms are arranged around often works better than one large sofa, because it creates two comfortable positions rather than one shared bench.

Scale: fitting the sofa to the room

The commonest scale error is a sofa that runs wall to wall. A gap of 15cm to 20cm at each end lets the wall read behind the furniture and stops the room feeling packed. The second error is pushing every piece against a wall, which produces a large empty middle and a set of conversations conducted across it. Pulling the sofa forward by even 10cm changes how a room feels, and in a long terraced reception room it allows the space behind to be used for a console or a lamp.

Keep 90cm on the main walkway and 40cm to 45cm between the sofa front and the coffee table. Where a room has to seat more people than one sofa can hold, a second smaller piece placed at an angle usually beats a longer sofa, because it creates a corner rather than a row. A chaise or day bed, chosen from a range of lounge chaise chairs UK rooms of awkward proportion can take, will often fill a difficult recess that no standard sofa suits.

Covers, cleaning and the label that has to be there

Every upholstered sofa sold for domestic use in the UK carries a permanent label confirming it meets the Furniture and Furnishings (Fire) (Safety) Regulations 1988. Check that it is present, particularly on second hand pieces. Beyond that, cleaning is a question of matching the cover to the household: removable covers for homes with children, wipeable surfaces for homes with pets or where laundering is impractical, and tight weaves anywhere claws are involved.

Sunlight is the quiet enemy. A sofa placed in front of a south facing window will fade unevenly along the top of the back, and no fabric is immune. Rotating and swapping seat cushions monthly evens out both fading and compression, and costs nothing.

What this means for UK homes

Measure yourself before you measure the room. Establish the seat depth and height that suit the people who will use the sofa most, then use those figures to filter the market. Check the frame, the suspension and the fill, because they determine whether the sofa still looks right in five years.

Then measure the room and the route into it. Leave 15cm to 20cm at each end of the wall, 90cm on the main walkway and 40cm to 45cm in front of the seat. Confirm the packed dimensions against the narrowest point of the journey from the front door. Finally, be honest about maintenance: buy foam if cushions will not be plumped, buy removable covers if spills are likely, and buy leather if the household would rather wipe than wash.

Methodology

This 2026 report reflects the editorial assessment of Furniture in Fashion as a UK modern furniture retailer, together with standard furniture dimensions, established upholstery construction practice and the UK regulations named in the text. It contains no proprietary sales data, no search data and no customer records, and no survey fieldwork was carried out. Generational differences are interpretations of typical housing circumstances and the priorities customers describe to us, not measured percentages.

Citing this report

Publications and websites may cite this analysis with credit to Furniture in Fashion as publisher and a link to Furniture in Fashion. Please present it as editorial research based on retail experience and standard specifications rather than as survey findings.

Frequently asked questions

What is a comfortable seat depth for a sofa?

Between 50cm and 55cm for upright sitting with proper back support, and 60cm or more if the sofa is mainly for lounging. Deeper seats need cushions behind the back for anyone who wants to sit upright.

What seat height should I look for?

Between 45cm and 50cm suits most adults and makes standing up straightforward. Lower seats feel relaxed but are harder to leave, which becomes more important the longer you own the sofa.

Is foam or feather better in sofa cushions?

High resilience foam keeps its shape with no effort and suits households that will not plump cushions. Feather is softer and more enveloping but needs regular plumping to look right. Fibre sits between the two and flattens faster than either.

How much space should I leave around a sofa?

About 90cm on the main route past it, 40cm to 45cm to the coffee table, and 15cm to 20cm at each end of the wall so the room does not look overfilled.

What should I check before buying an upholstered sofa in the UK?

Look for the permanent label confirming compliance with the Furniture and Furnishings (Fire) (Safety) Regulations 1988, ask what the frame is made from, ask whether the suspension is sprung or webbed, and confirm the packed dimensions against the narrowest doorway on the delivery route.

postTitle: Generation Gap: How Gen Z, Millennials and Boomers Choose TV Units
postContent:
A television unit is sized by the screen and positioned by the eye. Screen size is quoted as a diagonal, which tells you almost nothing useful about the furniture underneath, so the first job is converting it into a width. A 55 inch screen in the standard 16:9 shape measures roughly 122cm across, which means the unit beneath it should be at least 140cm wide if the television is not to look as though it is balancing on a plinth.

The second decision is height, and it is the one that causes physical discomfort rather than visual awkwardness. Seated eye level in a normal living room falls somewhere between 100cm and 120cm from the floor, and the centre of the screen should sit at or a little below that line. Every centimetre above it asks the neck to tilt back for the length of a film.

Key findings at a glance

  • Screen width, not diagonal, sets the minimum unit size. In 16:9 format, the screen width is approximately 0.87 times the quoted diagonal.
  • A unit should be wider than the screen by at least 20cm in total, and looks better with more.
  • Seated eye level generally falls between 100cm and 120cm, so the centre of the screen belongs at or slightly below that height.
  • Unit heights of 40cm to 55cm suit most large screens in a room where people watch from a sofa.
  • A soundbar needs 8cm to 12cm of clear height on the shelf it sits on, and must not block the screen's lower edge or its remote sensor.
  • Domestic storage furniture sold in the UK is covered by BS EN 14749, and any tall or top heavy unit should also be secured to the wall in homes with young children.
  • No public dataset records how UK households of different ages choose television furniture, so the differences here are read from room layouts and equipment rather than presented as measured data.

Converting a screen size into a piece of furniture

Televisions are sold on the diagonal of the panel, while furniture is sold on width. The conversion is straightforward geometry for any 16:9 screen, and it removes the guesswork entirely. Add a couple of centimetres for the bezel and the stand feet, which on many large screens sit close to the outer edges rather than in the centre.

43 inch95cm54cm115cm120cm to 140cm
50 inch111cm62cm130cm140cm to 160cm
55 inch122cm69cm140cm150cm to 180cm
65 inch144cm81cm165cm180cm to 200cm
75 inch166cm94cm185cm200cm to 240cm

Check the stand feet before ordering. Where the feet sit at the extreme corners of a large screen, the usable top surface of the unit has to be wider than the panel itself, and a pedestal stand in the centre needs a solid area of top rather than a slatted or glass shelf with a gap in the middle.

Height, eye level and the fireplace problem

Comfortable viewing depends on the relationship between the centre of the screen and the eyes of the person watching. Sit on your sofa and measure from the floor to your eyes: for most adults on a seat of 45cm, that lands somewhere between 100cm and 120cm. Then work backwards. On a 50cm unit, a 65 inch screen has its centre at roughly 90cm, which is slightly below eye level and comfortable. Put the same screen on a 90cm sideboard and the centre climbs to about 130cm, which is above eye level for almost everyone.

This is why televisions mounted above fireplaces so often disappoint. The mantel forces the screen up, and the neck compensates for the whole film. Where a chimney breast is the only sensible wall, the workable compromise is a lower profile unit sitting in the alcove line with the screen wall mounted just above it, rather than a full height installation above the mantel. Ranges of TV stands and units UK living rooms are arranged around include heights from around 35cm upwards precisely because screen sizes have grown while sofa heights have not.

The equipment behind the screen

A television unit is a cable management problem wearing a piece of furniture. Before choosing, count what has to live in it: a set top box, a games console, a router, a sound system, a streaming stick and the power supplies for all of them. Then check three things on the unit. First, the aperture size and position for cables, since a small hole at one end will not accept a plug. Second, the ventilation, because consoles and receivers generate heat and a sealed cabinet shortens their life. Third, whether the doors block the infrared sensors of anything inside them, which glass and mesh fronts avoid and solid doors do not.

Soundbars need their own allowance. Most require 8cm to 12cm of clear height, and they must sit below the bottom edge of the screen without intruding into the picture or covering the television's own remote sensor. Where the shelf is fixed, measure it before buying the soundbar rather than after. Units with a deeper top surface, such as those in entertainment units UK media rooms are built around, generally handle multi component setups better than slim consoles designed for a single screen.

Three households, three sets of requirements

In rented flats and first homes, the television unit is chosen with drilling ruled out. Wall mounting is rarely permitted, so the furniture has to carry the screen, and it usually has to carry a console and a router too. Low, wide and light is the pattern that works, along with open shelving that keeps equipment ventilated and accessible. A design that can be moved by one person matters more than it does in any other household, since the next room may be a different shape entirely.

Family households are storing far more than electronics. Games, controllers, cables and the accumulated contents of a living room all end up in the television unit, which makes closed storage the deciding feature. Stability is the other consideration: any unit that a child could climb should be secured to the wall with a restraint, and top heavy arrangements should be avoided entirely. Solid, low slung designs from a range of wooden TV stands UK family rooms use tend to be the steadiest option, since weight and a low centre of gravity work in your favour.

In long settled homes the priorities shift towards visibility and tidiness. A screen viewed from an armchair rather than a low sofa sits higher relative to the eye, so the unit can be taller. Cable clutter is a persistent irritation, so cabinets with concealed routing and closed backs are valued, as is a surface that wipes clean and reflects light in a room used mostly in the evening. That combination explains the continued appeal of high gloss TV stands UK sitting rooms are furnished with, though gloss finishes do show dust and fingerprints under lamplight.

Rooms that do not offer a straight wall

A great many British living rooms have a chimney breast, a bay window and a door in the remaining wall, which leaves no clean run for a large screen. Two solutions work. The first is an alcove arrangement, placing a lower unit in one alcove and treating the chimney breast as the backdrop. The second is a corner position, which uses the diagonal of the room and often produces a better viewing angle for a sofa set at an angle to the fireplace. Options among corner TV stands UK period homes rely on are built for exactly that geometry, with an angled back that sits flush across the corner.

Whichever is chosen, check the socket position first. A television placed where there is no socket produces either a trailing cable across a walkway or an unplanned electrical job, and both are avoidable with five minutes of measuring.

What this means for UK homes

Convert the screen diagonal into a width, add at least 20cm and treat that as the minimum unit size. Measure your seated eye level, subtract half the picture height and you have the maximum sensible height for the top of the unit. Those two figures narrow the choice faster than any style consideration.

Then plan the equipment. Count the boxes, check the cable apertures, confirm the ventilation and measure the soundbar shelf. In homes with children, fit a wall restraint and keep the heaviest items low. In rented homes, assume the screen sits on furniture rather than the wall. Get those decisions right and the unit will outlast at least two televisions, which is more than most living room furniture can claim.

Methodology

This 2026 report is based on the editorial assessment of Furniture in Fashion as a UK modern furniture retailer, together with standard furniture dimensions, the fixed geometry of 16:9 screen formats and named UK product safety standards where they apply to domestic storage furniture. Screen widths and picture heights are calculated from the standard 16:9 aspect ratio and rounded. No proprietary sales data, search data or customer records were used, and no survey fieldwork was carried out.

Citing this report

Journalists, editors and websites are welcome to cite this analysis with credit to Furniture in Fashion as publisher and a link to Furniture in Fashion. Please describe it as editorial research drawn from retail experience, screen geometry and published specifications rather than as survey data.

Frequently asked questions

How wide should a TV unit be for a 55 inch television?

At least 140cm. A 55 inch screen in 16:9 format measures around 122cm across, and a unit should extend beyond the screen by at least 20cm in total. Wider still looks more settled in the room.

How high should a TV unit be?

Usually 40cm to 55cm for a room where people watch from a sofa. Measure your seated eye level, which is commonly 100cm to 120cm, and aim to keep the centre of the screen at or slightly below it.

Is it a mistake to put a television above a fireplace?

It is a compromise. A mantel pushes the screen well above seated eye level, which means tilting the neck back throughout a film. Where the chimney breast is the only option, a lower unit with the screen mounted just above it is more comfortable than a full height installation.

How much space does a soundbar need?

Between 8cm and 12cm of clear shelf height for most models. Check that it does not cover the bottom edge of the screen or block the television's remote sensor, and measure the shelf before choosing the soundbar.

Should a TV unit be secured to the wall?

Any unit that is tall, top heavy or reachable by a young child should be fitted with an anti tip restraint. Domestic storage furniture in the UK is covered by BS EN 14749, and a wall fixing is a sensible precaution regardless of the design.
